title: A large-scale benchmarking of deterministic and stochastic derivative-free optimization algorithms
contribution: A March 2026 talk deck reruns the 2013 Rios-Sahinidis DFO benchmark with 42 implementations on 502 problems. It finds the group's own BAM best (81% solved at 2,500 evaluations, against 88% for the whole field), names an eight-solver minimal covering set, and rehearses a self-driving-lab use in silico (pp. 4-18).
problem_entry: Two entries. The first is the DOE PrOMMiS critical-minerals program, where a self-driving-lab loop sends black-box experiments to an optimizer (p. 2). The second is the observation that DFO results depend on problem type, dimension and budget, so studies disagree; a dated Scopus count sets DFO publications (≈100 in 2013, ≈340-370 a year in 2022-2025) against benchmarking studies (≈5-55 a year), and the question is posed as a large-scale, unified, reproducible benchmark (p. 3), entered through the group's own 2013 study (p. 4).
key_idea: Rerun the 2013 protocol on 42 implementations tagged same, updated or newly added, the group's own BAM among them (p. 5). The protocol keeps the 502-problem count, 2,500 evaluations and ten starting points, with success now judged on the median of 10 runs within max(1% relative, 0.01 absolute) of the global optimum (pp. 4, 7-8). The analysis adds family panels (direct/line search, trust region, branch-without-bound, others), dimension buckets, a virtual-best curve and a minimal covering set (pp. 10-16).
assumptions: 502 problems from minlp.com with n from 1 to 300 (20/26/24/30% in the buckets {1,2}, [3,9], [10,30], [31,300]), shown as convex or nonconvex and smooth or nonsmooth. The model is budget-only (2,500 evaluations) with 10 runs (pp. 7-8). Not stated: constraints, noise, the source of the global optima, seeds, options, versions, hardware. The application is a 4-variable reactor simulator, yield or E-factor optimized separately (p. 17).
experiments: Fraction-solved curves against evaluations. BAM 81% overall (≈0.59 at 500 evaluations); MULTIMIN ≈0.64, GLCCLUSTER ≈0.62, MCS ≈0.51, SID-PSM ≈0.41. Best rates by bucket 98/80/88/64%, virtual best 88% (100/91/93/72% by bucket). Minimal set BAM 404, GLCCLUSTER 23, MULTIMIN 4, MCS 2, SNOBFIT 2, CMAES 2, BOBYQA 1, DFSA 1. Bayesian-optimization codes below 0.10. Unchanged 2013 codes end near their 2013 curves. In silico, five solvers reach the reactor optimum in ≈50-100 evaluations. No times, versions, seeds, best runs or hold-out are shown (pp. 4, 9-17; chart values approximate).
positioning: Only the group's own 2013 study is named as an earlier benchmark (pp. 4-5). Other studies are invoked collectively, through a Scopus count and their 'inconsistent conclusions' (p. 3). The reactor model is credited to Hone et al. 2017 and Felton et al. 2021 (p. 17). BAM is listed as one more newly added code in the branch-without-bound family, and the slides do not say it is the authors' own (pp. 5, 11).
writing: Talk format with one red framing question (p. 3), titles that name findings, and colored headline numbers. Hedging is low ('outperformed all other algorithms', 'Minimal, irreducible set of dominating solvers', pp. 14, 18), and the success curves are called 'convergence rates' (p. 18). Slips: HOPSACK (p. 5); the p. 16 counts give 80.5% and 87.5% of 502 against the printed 81% and 88% (pp. 14, 16).
limits_future: Future work: more state-of-the-art DFO solvers and realistic critical-materials and minerals separation problems; BAM is about to be applied to separation processes (p. 18). No limits are stated. As read: no hold-out or developer rounds although the winner is the authors' solver; unnamed versions and options despite the 'reproducible' goal; median-only reporting; no stated source for the optima or constraint and noise scope; headline numbers at the maximum budget of 2,500 while the lab use is about 50 experiments (pp. 3, 8, 16-17).

method_links.note: Field-wide comparison of 42 codes on a large public library (502 problems from minlp.com) under identical budget and starting points. Success is defined explicitly against the global optimum on the median of 10 runs, and the verdict is a virtual-best ceiling plus a minimal covering portfolio of eight solvers.

The group's own BAM enters and is headlined as the single winner on 502 minlp.com problems, which note 03 §A2 identifies as a BAM development library. The slides mention none of the 2013 safeguards (hold-out, developer rounds, certified optima source, budget rationale; note 03 §B4). This is slide-level evidence for the step-7 hold-out gap flagged in Method 4 and for note 03 §C1.

One protocol kept for 13 years (502 problems, 2,500 evaluations, ten starting points), with solvers tagged same, updated or new; unchanged codes land near their 2013 curves. Versions and options are not named, short of Method 2's named builds and Heuristic 6.

The self-driving-lab framing sends the experimental black box straight to a DFO loop, and the demonstration optimizes a reactor simulator by DFO. No make-it-algebraic step is shown, and the slides do not say whether BAM builds models internally, so only Method 3's last clause (DFO for what stays black-box) is matched.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: in-silico rehearsal of a self-driving-lab campaign
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Five DFO solvers are run on a published reactor model (Hone et al. 2017; Felton et al. 2021) with four design variables and two objectives, the evaluations read as experiments ('50 evaluations (experiments) to optimize the system'), before BAM is applied to real critical-minerals separation.

Dated Scopus counts (5 December 2025) of DFO, black-box and zeroth-order publications against benchmarking studies, 2013-2025, frame the research question. The 2013 study argued from the growth in the number of solvers since the last comparison (note 01 §SW3).

transferable: Rerun an old benchmark with its problems, budget and starting points fixed and tag every solver same, updated or newly added; unchanged codes then act as a replication check (pp. 4-5, 8-9).
Score multi-run solvers on the median run against a known optimum with tolerance f(y) <= f(x*) + max(0.01|f(x*)|, 0.01), judging typical rather than lucky runs (p. 8).
Plot the virtual-best 'Solvable' curve next to the best single solver, overall and per dimension bucket (pp. 14-15).
Report the minimal covering portfolio as a stacked bar of marginal problem counts and state the budget at which it holds (p. 16).
Compare solvers within search-architecture families (direct/line search, trust region, branch-without-bound, others) before the all-solver plot (pp. 10-11).
Rehearse a self-driving-lab campaign on a published simulator of the experiment, reading evaluations as experiments, before committing a solver (p. 17).
coauthors: Donghyun Oh (first author; Georgia Tech, School of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering)

quotes.text: A problem was deemed “solved” if the median objective value over 10 runs was within 1% (relative) or 0.01 (absolute) of the global optimum
BAM with an 81% success rate outperformed all other algorithms
